notes.b: Blood is a tissue, like muscle or bone, but a liquid one. It is made of cells and cell fragments carried in a fluid, and each part has its own job.
points: Blood is a liquid tissue made of cells and cell fragments suspended in a liquid, the plasma. An adult has about 5 litres of blood.

If blood, with a chemical added to stop it clotting, is spun in a centrifuge (a machine that spins samples so the heaviest parts sink), it separates into about 55% plasma, a straw-coloured liquid on top, and about 45% cells.
The cells form a thin pale layer of white blood cells and platelets above a dark red layer of red blood cells at the bottom. Red blood cells make up nearly all of the cell volume.

Numbers in a healthy adult: red blood cells about 5 million per mm³ (cubic millimetre); white blood cells about 4,000 to 11,000 per mm³; platelets about 150,000 to 400,000 per mm³. Red cells therefore greatly outnumber white cells, by several hundred to one.

All blood cells and platelets are made in the red bone marrow, found in spongy bone such as the sternum, ribs, vertebrae, pelvis and the ends of long bones. They come from stem cells (unspecialised cells that can become other cell types) that divide by mitosis.

Functions of blood: transport (oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, wastes, hormones and heat), defence against infection, clotting to seal wounds, and keeping the internal environment steady (pH, temperature and water balance).

Diagram: a stained blood smear under a light microscope. Draw many red blood cells (pale centres, no nucleus), one or two white blood cells (larger, with a stained nucleus: a phagocyte with a lobed nucleus and a lymphocyte with a large round nucleus) and small platelets. Label each.
Diagram: draw a centrifuged tube labelled plasma, white cells and platelets layer, and red cells layer, with percentages.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name the components of blood and give a function of each. Learn the four: plasma, red cells, white cells and platelets.

notes.b: Plasma is the liquid part of blood, and everything else in blood is carried in it or by it. Because it is mostly water, it can dissolve and transport a huge range of substances around the body.
points: Plasma is about 90% water, with substances dissolved or suspended in it. Water is a good solvent, so many substances dissolve in it, and it also carries heat.

Dissolved substances transported in plasma: nutrients (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol, vitamins and minerals); wastes (urea, from the liver to the kidneys, and most of the carbon dioxide); hormones; and salts, such as sodium, chloride, calcium and hydrogencarbonate ions.
Carbon dioxide is carried mostly in the plasma as hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻). They form in red blood cells, by the enzyme carbonic anhydrase (CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻).
A small amount of carbon dioxide is simply dissolved in plasma, and some is carried by haemoglobin. There is more on this in CO₂ as a controlling factor in breathing.

Plasma proteins: fibrinogen and other clotting factors, for clotting; antibodies, for defence against pathogens; and albumin, which holds water in the blood by osmosis and carries some substances. Serum is plasma with the clotting proteins removed.
Plasma distributes heat from active organs, such as working muscles, around the body. Its hydrogencarbonate and protein buffers (chemicals that resist changes in acidity) keep the blood pH near 7.4.
notes.tip: When asked what plasma carries, list specific substances: glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones, most of the carbon dioxide, and heat. Do not just say 'nutrients'.

notes.b: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to every cell in the body. Almost every feature of their structure helps them do that one job well.
points: Red blood cells, or erythrocytes, are biconcave discs (round and thinner in the centre than at the edge), about 7 to 8 µm across. They carry oxygen from the lungs to all body cells.
The biconcave shape gives a large surface area for their volume, so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly, and every part of the cell is close to the surface.
There is no nucleus, and no mitochondria, in the mature cell, which leaves more room for haemoglobin. The cell is also packed with haemoglobin, so each cell can carry a lot of oxygen.
The cell is small and flexible, so it squeezes through capillaries in single file, close to the capillary wall. This shortens the distance oxygen must diffuse.
Because they have no mitochondria, red blood cells respire anaerobically (without oxygen), so they do not use up the oxygen they carry.

Haemoglobin is a red protein made of four polypeptide chains, each with a haem group containing iron, so each haemoglobin molecule can carry four oxygen molecules. In the lungs, where oxygen is plentiful, haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin, which is bright red.
In respiring tissues, where oxygen is low, oxyhaemoglobin releases its oxygen. The reaction is reversible. Haemoglobin + oxygen ⇌ oxyhaemoglobin.
notes.tip: For 'relate structure to function', pair each feature with its reason: biconcave gives a large surface area for fast diffusion, no nucleus gives more room for haemoglobin. Haemoglobin carries the oxygen, so say that it combines with oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.

notes.h: Life cycle and health links of red blood cells
notes.b: Red blood cells wear out and must be constantly replaced. Problems with their number or with haemoglobin affect how much oxygen reaches the tissues.
points: Red blood cells are made in the red bone marrow and live about 120 days. With no nucleus they cannot repair themselves, so they wear out.
Old cells are broken down in the liver and spleen. The iron is recycled to make new haemoglobin, and the rest of the haem is converted into bile pigments, which are excreted in bile.
The kidney hormone EPO stimulates the production of red blood cells. There is more on this in Hormonal manipulation.
Anaemia is a shortage of red blood cells or haemoglobin, so less oxygen is carried, causing tiredness and pale skin. A common cause is iron deficiency, because iron is needed to make haem.
Carbon monoxide, in cigarette smoke and from faulty gas appliances, combines with haemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen does, so less oxygen is carried and it can kill.
Sickle-cell anaemia is a further disorder of red blood cells, named here only.
notes.tip: Exams ask where blood cells are made, how long red cells live (about 120 days) and to explain anaemia. For anaemia, link the shortage of red cells or haemoglobin to less oxygen carried.

notes.b: White blood cells are the body's defenders against infection. They differ from red cells in several ways, which makes a good comparison to learn.
points: White blood cells, or leucocytes, defend the body against infection. Unlike red blood cells, they have a nucleus, are larger and colourless (they have no haemoglobin), and are far fewer in number.
They are made in the red bone marrow, and many can squeeze out through capillary walls into the tissues, where infections often are.
There are two broad groups: phagocytes, which engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis), and lymphocytes, which produce antibodies or kill infected cells.
The number of white cells rises during an infection, so a white cell count is used in diagnosing infections. Leukaemia is a cancer of the white-cell-forming cells.
notes.tip: If asked for one difference between red and white blood cells, pick a clear one: white cells have a nucleus and red cells do not, or white cells have no haemoglobin.

notes.b: Platelets are not whole cells but fragments, and they are the first responders when a blood vessel is damaged.
points: Platelets, or thrombocytes, are small fragments of cytoplasm enclosed in membrane, with no nucleus. They break off from large cells in the red bone marrow.
Platelets live about 7 to 10 days and start the clotting of blood.
Clotting matters because it stops blood loss from a damaged vessel and seals the wound so that pathogens cannot enter. It is part of the first line of defence against infection.
notes.tip: Exams ask for the role of platelets in clotting: they stick at the damage and release clotting factors.

notes.b: Clotting is a chain of events in which one change triggers the next, ending in a mesh of protein threads that plugs the wound. Learn the stages in order.
points: 1. A blood vessel is damaged.
2. Platelets stick to the exposed damaged wall and to each other, forming a temporary plug.
3. The platelets and damaged tissue release clotting factors.
4. A series of reactions, needing calcium ions and clotting proteins made in the liver with the help of vitamin K, converts the inactive plasma protein prothrombin into the active enzyme thrombin.
5. Thrombin converts the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble threads of fibrin.
6. The fibrin threads form a mesh that traps red blood cells and platelets, forming a clot.

7. At the surface the clot dries and hardens into a scab, under which the tissue repairs. Calcium and vitamin K are both needed for clotting. Haemophilia is an inherited disorder in which a clotting factor is missing.

An unwanted clot inside a vessel, a thrombosis, can block an artery and cause a heart attack or stroke. Diagram: a flow chart of damage, platelets, clotting factors (with Ca²⁺ and vitamin K), prothrombin, thrombin, fibrinogen, fibrin mesh and clot. Add fibrin threads trapping red blood cells.
notes.tip: Keep the two protein changes straight: prothrombin becomes thrombin, and thrombin then converts fibrinogen into fibrin. Do not confuse clotting (fibrin forming) with agglutination (antibodies clumping red cells).

notes.b: Your ABO blood group depends on molecules on the surface of your red blood cells. The plasma then carries antibodies matched to whichever molecules your own cells lack.
points: A blood group is set by the antigens on the surface membrane of a person's red blood cells. An antigen is a molecule that can trigger an immune response. In the ABO system there are two antigens, A and B.
The plasma naturally contains antibodies against the ABO antigen or antigens that a person's own red cells lack. This stops the body attacking its own cells.
Group A has antigen A on the red cells and anti-B antibodies in the plasma. Group B has antigen B and anti-A antibodies.
Group AB has both antigens and no antibodies. Group O has no antigens and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
Agglutination: if red cells carrying an antigen meet the matching antibody, for example A cells meeting anti-A, the antibodies bind to the antigens and stick the cells together in clumps.
In a transfusion the clumps can block small blood vessels, and the donor cells are destroyed, or burst. This can cause kidney failure and death.

Diagram: four red blood cells, one for each group, showing the antigens on the membrane (A, B, both, none), with the antibodies in the plasma written beside each. Add a sketch of agglutination, with antibodies linking red cells into a clump.
notes.tip: Antigens are on the red cells and antibodies are in the plasma. Group O has no antigens but both antibodies; group AB has both antigens but no antibodies. Students often swap these.

notes.b: Transfusion works only if the donor's red cells do not meet an antibody in the recipient's plasma that matches their antigens. The rule follows from the ABO antigens and antibodies.
points: What matters is the donor's red-cell antigens and the recipient's antibodies. A recipient can safely receive red cells that carry no antigen against which their own plasma has antibodies.
Group O red cells carry no antigens, so they can be given to anyone, and group O is called the universal donor. This applies to red cells: group O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B.
Group AB people have no antibodies, so they can receive red cells of any ABO group, and group AB is the universal recipient. In practice, hospitals give the same group whenever possible.
Compatibility: group O can receive O only; group A can receive A or O; group B can receive B or O; group AB can receive A, B, AB or O.

Blood-group testing: a drop of blood is mixed separately with anti-A serum and with anti-B serum. Clumping with anti-A only means group A; clumping with anti-B only means group B; clumping with both means AB; clumping with neither means O.
A third test, with anti-D, tests the Rhesus group.
notes.tip: Exams ask for universal donor and recipient and why compatibility matters. Argue from antigens and antibodies: O red cells have no antigens to be attacked, and AB plasma has no antibodies to attack them.

notes.b: The Rhesus factor is a second red-cell antigen system, on top of ABO. Unlike the ABO antibodies, the Rhesus antibody has to be learned by the immune system first.
points: The Rhesus (Rh) factor is another red-cell antigen, the D antigen. People whose red cells carry it are Rhesus positive (Rh+), and those without it are Rhesus negative (Rh−).
A person's full blood group combines both systems, for example O negative or A positive.

Unlike anti-A and anti-B, anti-D antibodies are not naturally present. A Rh− person makes them only after Rh+ red cells enter their blood, for example through a transfusion of Rh+ blood or during pregnancy.
A first exposure therefore does little harm, but a second exposure triggers a rapid, strong attack on Rh+ cells. So Rh− patients must receive Rh− blood.
notes.tip: Remember that anti-D is not present naturally, so a Rh− person must be exposed first.

notes.b: A Rhesus negative mother carrying a Rhesus positive baby can become sensitised to her baby's blood, and that may endanger a later baby. The problem is called haemolytic disease of the newborn, and it can be prevented.
points: 1. A Rh− mother carries a Rh+ baby, inherited from a Rh+ father.
2. Normally the blood of mother and fetus does not mix, but at birth, or after a miscarriage, abortion or injury, some fetal red cells enter the mother's blood.
3. Her immune system makes anti-D antibodies and memory cells, and she is now sensitised. The first baby is usually unaffected, because it is born before many antibodies are made.
4. In a later pregnancy with a Rh+ baby, her anti-D antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the fetus's red blood cells.
5. The baby can suffer severe anaemia and jaundice, brain damage or death.
Prevention: a Rh− mother is given an injection of anti-D antibodies, anti-D immunoglobulin, during pregnancy and within 72 hours after the birth of a Rh+ baby, or after a miscarriage or injury.

These antibodies destroy any fetal Rh+ cells in her blood before her own immune system can respond, so she does not make her own anti-D or memory cells. The injected antibodies are broken down over a few weeks.
This is artificial passive immunity (antibodies given ready-made, not made by the body). Every pregnant woman's blood group is tested early in pregnancy for this reason.
notes.tip: The danger is to a Rh+ baby of a Rh− mother, not the reverse, and usually to a second or later baby. Include the anti-D injection within 72 hours of birth when asked how it is prevented.

notes.h: The value of knowing blood groups for health
notes.b: Knowing a person's blood group saves lives in several ways, from transfusions to pregnancy care. Each use below comes from knowing the groups.
points: Safe blood transfusion: before a transfusion, the patient's ABO and Rhesus groups are tested, and the donor blood is cross-matched, meaning it is mixed with the patient's plasma to check that no clumping occurs.
This prevents fatal transfusion reactions and allows transfusions in surgery, after accidents, in childbirth, for anaemia and in cancer treatment.

Emergencies: group O Rh− red cells are given when there is no time to test the patient, because they carry no A, B or D antigens. Only a minority of people are O negative, so their donations are especially valuable.
Pregnancy: identifying Rh− mothers and giving anti-D has made haemolytic disease of the newborn rare.
Blood donation: knowing which groups are needed lets the blood service plan donor sessions and stocks. Donors of all groups are needed, because blood can be stored only for a limited time.
In Ireland, donations are collected and tested by the Irish Blood Transfusion Service, and donated blood is screened for infections.
Organ and bone-marrow transplants: donors and recipients are matched for ABO group and tissue type to reduce the chance of rejection.

Nature of Science: before blood groups were known, transfusions often killed patients. Karl Landsteiner discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901, for which he received the Nobel Prize in 1930, which made safe transfusion possible.
In 1940 Landsteiner and Alexander Wiener described the Rhesus factor, named after the rhesus monkeys whose blood was used in the experiments.
notes.tip: For 'the value of knowing blood groups', give at least two uses with reasons, such as safe transfusion and preventing haemolytic disease of the newborn.

keyTerms.definition: A red blood cell: a biconcave, anucleate cell packed with haemoglobin that carries oxygen.
A red iron-containing protein in red blood cells that combines reversibly with oxygen.
Haemoglobin combined with oxygen, formed in the lungs, which releases its oxygen in respiring tissues.
The straw-coloured liquid part of blood, about 90% water, which carries cells, nutrients, wastes, hormones and heat.
Plasma with the clotting proteins removed.
A small fragment of cytoplasm, with no nucleus, that starts the clotting of blood.
An inactive plasma protein that is converted into the active enzyme thrombin during clotting.
The insoluble protein threads, formed from fibrinogen, that make up the mesh of a blood clot.
A molecule on a cell surface that can trigger an immune response, such as A and B on red blood cells.
A protein in the plasma that binds to a specific antigen.
The clumping of red cells caused by antibodies binding to antigens on their surface.
Group O, whose red cells carry no A, B or D antigens and can be given to anyone.
Group AB, whose plasma has no antibodies against A or B, so it can receive red cells of any ABO group.
The D antigen on red blood cells; people who carry it are Rhesus positive.
An antibody against the D antigen, given by injection to Rh− mothers to prevent sensitisation.
The destruction of a Rh+ fetus’s red blood cells by anti-D antibodies from a sensitised Rh− mother.
Immunity given by injected antibodies, rather than made by the person’s own immune system.

questions.prompt: Give two features of red blood cells and explain how each suits them to carrying oxygen.
questions.model: Feature 1: red blood cells are biconcave discs. This shape gives a large surface area for their volume, so oxygen diffuses in and out quickly, and every part of the cell is close to the surface. Feature 2: the mature cell has no nucleus and is packed with haemoglobin. The lack of a nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin, and each haemoglobin molecule carries four oxygen molecules, so the cell carries a large amount of oxygen. Haemoglobin combines with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases the oxygen in respiring tissues. Red blood cells are also small and flexible, so they pass through capillaries in single file, close to the capillary wall, which helps oxygen to diffuse out.

questions.prompt: Explain the ABO blood group system and why a person of blood group A cannot safely receive blood from a person of group B. Explain why knowledge of blood groups is important for health.
questions.model: In the ABO system, a blood group is set by the antigens on the red blood cells: A, B, both (AB) or neither (O). The plasma contains antibodies against the antigens that the person’s own red cells lack. A person of group A has antigen A on their red cells and anti-B antibodies in their plasma. Group B blood has B antigens on its red cells. When the donor’s B cells meet the recipient’s anti-B antibodies, the antibodies bind to the B antigens and stick the cells together in clumps, a process called agglutination. The clumps can block small blood vessels, and the donor cells are destroyed, which can cause kidney failure and death. Knowing blood groups is important for health because blood is matched before transfusion, so that transfusions are safe, and group O Rh− red cells can be given in emergencies when a patient cannot be tested. Blood groups also matter for pregnancy, because identifying Rh− mothers and giving anti-D prevents haemolytic disease of the newborn. They are also used to match organ and bone-marrow donors and recipients to reduce rejection.

questions.prompt: Explain why a Rhesus negative mother who has had a Rhesus positive baby may be given an injection of anti-D after the birth.
questions.model: At birth some of the baby’s red blood cells, which are Rh+, can enter the mother’s blood. Her immune system then makes anti-D antibodies and memory cells, so she becomes sensitised. In a later pregnancy with a Rh+ baby, her anti-D antibodies can cross the placenta and destroy the baby’s red blood cells, causing haemolytic disease of the newborn. The injection of anti-D antibodies given after the birth destroys any fetal Rh+ cells in her blood before her own immune system can respond. So she does not make her own anti-D or memory cells, and the risk to a later baby is prevented. This is an example of artificial passive immunity, because the antibodies are injected rather than made by her own immune system.
